lead: Decode, convert and analyse data in your web browser by chaining small operations into a recipe. CyberChef was built by GCHQ and is used for encodings, hashes, compression, encryption and many other tasks.
use_when: You found a string that looks encoded, such as Base64 or hex, and want to see what it hides.
You need to convert data between formats, or decode several layers one after another.
You want to repeat the same set of steps on many inputs and save the steps as a recipe.

features.title: Recipe workflow
items: Four areas on screen: Input, Output, a list of Operations and your Recipe
Drag operations into the recipe and set their options
The output updates by itself whenever the input or recipe changes (Bake)
Breakpoints let you stop at one step and go through the recipe step by step

features.title: Magic
items: The Magic operation tries to find out how data is encoded and which operations can decode it
It runs in the background, and an icon appears in the Output when it finds a useful decoding
It has settings for depth, intensive mode and more languages

features.title: Wide set of operations
items: Encodings such as Base64, hexdumps and character sets
Encryption and decryption such as AES, DES and Blowfish, and XOR
Parsing of IPv6 addresses and X.509 certificates

features.title: Handling files and sharing
items: Drop files of up to 2 GB onto the input box
Save the output to a file
Save recipes in the browser, or share a link that contains the recipe and input
Selecting text shows its offset and length and highlights it in the other box

requirements: A modern web browser. The project lists Chrome 50 or newer and Firefox 38 or newer. The project states that recipes and input are not sent to the CyberChef server, because everything runs in your browser. For offline use you can download a copy from the link in the app, run the project's Docker image, or build it from source with Node.js.

steps.title: Decide online or offline
steps.text: The public site runs in your browser and does not send your data to the server, according to the project. For case data, many labs still prefer a local copy. Use the download link at the top left of the app to get a full copy you can run offline.

steps.title: Or run it with Docker
steps.text: If Docker Desktop is running, start the project's ready-made image. Then open the address in your browser.

steps.title: Open the page and add input
steps.text: Open the CyberChef page (http://localhost:8080 for the Docker version). Paste your text into the Input box, or drop a file onto it.

steps.title: Find an operation
steps.text: Use the search box above the operation list. Type part of a name, such as base64. Double-click the operation, or drag it into the Recipe area.

steps.title: Let Magic help
steps.text: If you do not know the encoding, look for the magic icon in the Output box. Hover over it to see a suggested recipe and a preview. Click it to add those operations to your recipe.

steps.title: Chain more steps
steps.text: Add further operations below the first. Each one works on the result of the one above. Use a breakpoint on a step to see its output on its own, if the final result looks wrong.

steps.title: Save the work
steps.text: Save the output to a file, and save the recipe, or copy the link that holds the recipe and input. Write the recipe steps in your case notes so another person can repeat them.

cases.title: Decoding suspicious strings
cases.why: Layers of Base64, hex and similar encodings in scripts or logs can be peeled off one at a time, or tried automatically with Magic.

cases.title: Malware and script triage
cases.why: Obfuscated commands can be decoded and read without running them, using operations such as XOR and decompression.

cases.title: Converting data for other tools
cases.why: Turn timestamps, hex dumps or encoded values into a form that a report or another tool can use.

cases.title: Hashing text and small files
cases.why: Compute common hashes of a string or small file quickly, for a check or a lookup.

cases.title: Certificates and network data
cases.why: Parse X.509 certificates and IPv6 addresses to read their fields.

cases.title: Teaching encodings
cases.why: The step-by-step recipe view helps students see how each encoding changes the data.

strengths: Free and open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.
Needs no install for the online version, and has an offline option.
The project reports that all processing happens in the browser.
Recipes can be saved and shared, so work is easy to repeat.
limits: It works on data you give it, such as text and files. It does not collect evidence or read disk images.
Magic gives likely answers, not certain ones. Check each suggested decoding yourself.
Very large inputs can be slow in a browser. You can switch off automatic baking when the input is large.
Dropped files are limited to 2 GB, according to the project.
Beginners may find the long list of operations confusing. Use the search box.
Do not paste sensitive case data into a copy you do not control. Use a local copy.

works_with.note: Break down URLs and decode timestamps inside them
Identify the type of a hash you found
Extract hidden strings, then decode them here
Pull out macro code, then decode its strings
